chunks: And from him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Asimī, from Ali ibn al-Hasan al-Taymulī, from Ali ibn Asbāt, from Ibrahim ibn Abi al-Bilād, that Abdullah ibn Junbub said:

I was at the Standing (at Arafat), and when I departed, I went to Ibrahim ibn Shu'ayb and greeted him. He was afflicted with the loss of one of his eyes, and his healthy eye was red, as if it were a clot of blood. I said to him, 'You have lost one of your eyes, and by Allah, I am concerned for the other, so if you wept a little less.' He said, 'No, by Allah, O Abu Muhammad, I did not make a supplication for myself today.' I said, 'Then for whom did you supplicate?' He said, 'I supplicated for my brothers, because I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: "Whoever supplicates for his brother in his absence, Allah appoints for him an angel who says, and for you is the like."' So I wanted to be the one supplicating for my brothers, and the angel to be supplicating for me, because I am in doubt regarding my own supplication, and I am not in doubt regarding the angel's supplication for me.

key_terms.أَبَا عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Abu Abdillah, a title for Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him)
key_terms.الْمَوْقِف: The Standing at Arafat, a central ritual of Hajj
key_terms.بِظَهْرِ الْغَيْبِ: In his absence / behind his back

ai.seo_question: Why did Ibrahim ibn Shu'ayb choose to supplicate for others instead of himself during Hajj?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the spiritual psychology of the Arafat stand, where Ibrahim ibn Shu'ayb prioritized the certainty of divine angels over his own self-doubt. It illustrates the Shia scholarly emphasis on *tawakkul* (trust in God) and the efficacy of intercessory prayer, rooted in the Prophet’s and Imams’ teachings that angels reciprocate blessings for others with equal blessings for the supplicant.
